name: Sickly Green
lede: Sickly green is a yellowish green with a bad reputation, the color of faded flesh paint in old pictures and of the alien and the ill in twentieth-century culture.

sections.title: When the pink faded
sections.body:
Finlay notes that when pinkish pigments fade from an old painting, the faces can be left a sickly green [1]. Roman and Byzantine artists liked the look, and their mosaic faces set green stones among pink ones to cool a ruddy complexion [1]. Terre verte underpainting of flesh, popularized by Giotto according to a source cited by Finlay, continued spasmodically until Tiepolo in the eighteenth century [1].

Jarman argues that the Cold War Fifties invented a different green, not of birth but alien, the color of pus and rotting flesh, which gave us phrases like green around the gills [2]. It is a personal essay's claim rather than a measured finding.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in only 3 works, including two by Niels Larsen Stevns, from 1908 and 1941 [3]. As always these are photographs of varnished paintings, so read them as screen colors [3].

notes.cite: ColorHub archive, 23,781 museum paintings as photographed (tools/article_field.py, dE2000 <= 6, >= 5% of canvas)

questions.q: What did Roman and Byzantine mosaicists mix with pink stones in faces?
Which decade does Jarman say invented an alien, rotten green?

openers: Some old faces are green because their pink flesh paint faded; Byzantine mosaicists used green stones on purpose.
